newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Good value to be gained from Germany.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Good value to be gained from Germany.

text.p: Bunds will present good value over the coming weeks and their allure could lead to outperformance against U.S. Treasuries, analysts said on Wednesday.
Technical gains, which have helped to underpin the recent firm tone in the German market, pushed December Bund futures traded on LIFFE to a new all-time high at 101.56 earlier in the session.

"Bunds will start outperforming and we'll probably see the spread moving to about 80 basis points during the first quarter of next year," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.
The 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread is currently at 43 basis points having pulled in from around 80 basis points in late September.
Lewis said U.S. Treasury yields would probably go up relative to German yields as a result of the combined effects of current economic situations in Germany and the U.S.
"As Issing was saying overnight, there aren't many signs of inflation pressures in the Germany at the moment," he said.

Speaking at a conference in Munich on Tuesday, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said the shortfall on the Bundesbank's targets for German M3 growth in 1996 would be below October's M3 growth of 8.4 percent.

Robin Marshall, chief econmist at Chase in London agreed, saying the key difference was the different positions of Germany and U.S. in the economic cycle, although there was not likely to be a change in official monetary policy in either country for some time.

"There is almost a 180 degree difference, in the sense that Germany is struggling to come out of a period of weak growth, whereas U.S. is probably coming out of a period of strong growth, and may be about to slow down a bit," he said. "That probably means yields may actually fall in both markets."
Marshall said the market would be driven by relative value considerations rather than changes in domestic policy.
"With the low inflationary outlook in Germany and a fairly steep curve, the 10-year area of the market is probably pretty good value," he said.
At 1310 GMT, 6.25 percent Bund due April 2006, was trading at 103.30 to yield 5.77 percent.
Lewis said 10-year Bund yields could get down to around 5.75 percent on an annual basis, the equivalent of around 5.55-5.60 percent semi-annually.
U.S. Treasuries' coupon payments are calculated on a semi- annual basis.

"It is true that once they go below six it does become heavy weather trying to get them much lower, but I would see them down to five and three-quarters on an annual basis," he said. "We have seen them down at that level on previous occasions in recent years."

Marshall said Bunds had been overshadowed by convergence within European bonds in the run up to European Economic and Monetary Union, resulting in German underperformance, but further convergence could be difficult.

"You may get some profit taking on convergence trades and that will help Bunds. There will also be some incentive for traders to lock in profits between now and year-end as people start worrying about year-end bonuses," he said.
But some analysts saw a likely pick-up in German economic growth in 1997 and further narrowing of the T-bond/Bund spread.
"I would target 25 basis points for the first part of 1997," said Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank in London.
He said the T-note/Bund yield gap had a strong correlation with the currencies, so any losses in Bunds could be offset by gains from investing in marks.
"To put it another way, if you prefer Treasuries you should do so on a hedged basis," he said.
